title: Read the config that actually governs where journald writes
explanation: `cat /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/*.conf` shows a drop-in setting `Storage=volatile` — journald is keeping logs only under `/run` (tmpfs, RAM-backed), which is wiped on every reboot by definition. This is why `journalctl -b -1` has nothing: the previous boot's journal never touched disk.

title: Persistence needs two things to both be true, not one
explanation: With the default `Storage=auto`, journald persists to disk only if `/var/log/journal` exists — otherwise it silently falls back to volatile. Setting `Storage=persistent` (or `auto` plus creating the directory) tells journald to write to disk; the directory has to exist for that to actually happen, since journald won't create it on its own.

title: Fix both halves: the setting and the directory
explanation: Edit `/etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/volatile.conf` to `Storage=persistent`, and `sudo mkdir -p /var/log/journal` — skipping either one leaves journald exactly where it started.

title: Restart and explicitly migrate what's already in memory
explanation: `sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald` applies the new config, but the logs already sitting in the volatile `/run` journal from the current boot don't move to disk automatically until the next boot's `systemd-journal-flush.service` runs. `sudo journalctl --flush` forces that migration immediately instead of waiting for a reboot.

title: Verify the files exist on disk where you expect them
explanation: `ls -R /var/log/journal` should now show a `<machine-id>/system.journal` file, and `journalctl --header` reports that path rather than one under `/run` — confirming journald is genuinely writing to persistent storage, not just configured to.
